why: Sorting both parts gives a sorted whole exactly when every left value is <= every right value, i.e. max(A[0..i-1]) <= min(A[i..n-1]). That is a prefix-maximum / suffix-minimum scan, the 'prefix aggregate' idea with max and min instead of sums.
hints: After sorting each part, the only place the joined array can go wrong is the seam between the two parts.
The split before index i works iff the largest element on the left is at most the smallest element on the right.
Precompute suffix minima right to left, then sweep left to right with a running prefix maximum and count split points i in 1..n-1 where prefixMax <= suffixMin[i]. O(n).
pitfalls: Both parts must be non-empty: split points are 1..n-1 only.
Use <= (non-decreasing): equal values across the seam are fine.
Re-sorting for each split is O(n^2 log n) and too slow.
statement:
You are given an array A of N integers. Choose a split point to cut it into a non-empty left part and a non-empty right part. Sort each part independently, then join them back (left first). Count the split points for which the joined array is sorted in non-decreasing order.

Example: A = [1, 3, 2, 4].

  • Left [1], right [3,2,4]: sorted parts [1] + [2,3,4] = [1,2,3,4]. Sorted.
  • Left [1,3], right [2,4]: [1,3] + [2,4] = [1,3,2,4]. Not sorted.
  • Left [1,3,2], right [4]: [1,2,3] + [4] = [1,2,3,4]. Sorted.

The answer is 2.
